stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 20): YTL Power International Bhd’s (KL:YTLPOWR) data centre in Johor was reportedly part of an arrangement that allowed Chinese technology giant Alibaba to remotely access Nvidia chips through a network of regional companies, a *New York Times* (*NYT*) report alleges.

The report comes amid assurances from YTL Power’s management that the group was not involved in alleged chip diversion activities linked to Singapore-based Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, according to investment analysts who attended the group's results briefing on Thursday.

In a report, Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) said management told analysts it was not under investigation over the matter.

According to the *NYT* report dated Nov 18, Alibaba agreed to become a customer of Megaspeed, which used the agreement to secure funding to purchase Nvidia chips.

Megaspeed subsequently partnered with data centre operators such as YTL to house and operate the chips.

At YTL’s facility, Megaspeed’s subsidiary, Speedmatrix, operated the Nvidia chips on Alibaba’s behalf, according to *NYT* citing five people familiar with the project who were not authorised to speak publicly.

The alleged arrangement allowed Alibaba and its customers to access the chips remotely through YTL’s data centre.

Some chips intended for the facilities were allegedly smuggled into China despite US export restrictions, the report said.

Data from the Malaysian facility was allegedly transmitted through fibre-optic cables to an internet hub in Singapore before being routed to China through undersea cables.

US officials believe China's military uses overseas data centres to train artificial intelligence (AI) models before running them from facilities within China.

*The Edge* has reached out to YTL Power for comment on the *NYT* report.

On Thursday, YTL Power said it is planning further data centre investments after the segment recorded a sharp increase in earnings in its first quarter ended Sept 30, 2026 (1QFY2027).

The data centre segment's profit before tax surged nearly 133 times to RM139.54 million from RM1.05 million a year earlier, while revenue jumped 491.35% to RM329.38 million from RM55.7 million.

The business has become the group's third-largest earnings contributor, after power generation and water.

Despite the controversy and tighter US restrictions on advanced chip exports, research houses remain broadly positive on YTL Power's data centre prospects, citing its infrastructure, customer commitments and potential demand from new clients.

RHB Research said management intends to focus on leasing data centre space rather than directly providing AI computing services, amid tighter US restrictions on Chinese companies accessing advanced chips remotely.

Under this model, YTL Power provides the space, electricity and cooling infrastructure, while customers operate their own equipment.

RHB also noted that existing customer agreements were backed by bank guarantees covering long-term commitments for electricity and data centre space. These provide some protection against potential losses if customers terminate their contracts early.

The research house maintained its 'buy' recommendation and target price of RM7.

HLIB shared a similar outlook, citing YTL Power's secured land, electricity supply and existing infrastructure as key advantages in supporting further data centre expansion.

It maintained its 'buy' call and target price of RM8.08, viewing the recent share price weakness as an opportunity for investors.

Meanwhile, CGS International (CGSI) said YTL Power was receiving more enquiries from US-based companies seeking data centre space, despite uncertainty surrounding US chip export restrictions.

It noted that the group's direct AI computing services business remained relatively small at 10MW and was backed by Nvidia.

However, CGSI adopted a more cautious outlook on future expansion, lowering its assumed data centre capacity to 500MW from 850MW amid regulatory uncertainty.

CGSI cut its target price to RM5.70 from RM6.50 but maintained its 'add' recommendation.

YTL Power currently has 298MW of contracted data centre capacity, of which 160MW was operational as at end-September. The group is also seeking customers for another 200MW of capacity, which is expected to be completed in the second half of 2027.

YTL Power, which had been under selling pressure after Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia, fell 15 sen to RM3.85 as at 3pm on Friday despite the strong profit results on Thursday.

YTL Power’s shares have fallen 27.4% over the past month, from RM5.32 on Oct 30 to RM3.85 on Friday, wiping out about RM12.92 billion in market capitalisation.

stories.summary: Australian data centre company Nextdc has vowed not to develop sites near residential areas after community opposition and power constraints delayed a major expansion project.

stories.title_zh: NextDC表示将不再在居民区附近开发数据中心
stories.content:
(Nov 20): Australian data centre company Nextdc has vowed not to develop sites near residential areas after community opposition and power constraints delayed a major expansion project.

The company last month said its M3 expansion in Melbourne had been delayed after community protests prompted power company Jemena to pause the installation of power poles. The news sparked Nextdc’s biggest single-day share price slump on record.

“There’s growing opposition to data centres in Australia and worldwide,” outgoing chairman Douglas Flynn said at the company’s annual meeting Friday in Sydney. “We do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential properties.”

The fallout from the M3 problems has deepened shareholder tensions. Some 72% of votes were cast against the company’s remuneration plan — the second straight year investors have largely rejected the company’s pay plan. Still, shareholders voted against spilling the board, a ballot triggered when more than 25% of votes oppose the remuneration report for two consecutive years.

Shares fell as much as 5.5% in Sydney trading on Friday, even as the company gave a slight upgrade to its revenue and earnings guidance.

“Would we buy this site again tomorrow? No we wouldn’t,” said Flynn, referring to M3, adding that the final development wouldn’t be “as ugly” as the original industrial site that had long been there. He said the board was working closely with Jemena regarding M3 and a path forward.

Nextdc has paused new commitments and plans to only commit new capital selectively, focusing on projects with customer contracts, expected returns above its cost of capital, sufficiently advanced power and planning, as well as funding in place.

Following the M3 delay, chief executive officer Craig Scroggie last month gave up his short-term and long-term bonuses for the 2027 financial year, while the company’s non-executive directors agreed to a 10% reduction in their fees.

The board also withdrew a resolution to seek shareholder approval to boost the maximum annual remuneration of non-executive directors to A$2.5 million (RM6.85 million) from A$2.2 million.

Asked on Friday about potential strategy changes at Nvidia Corp following founder Jensen Huang’s departure, Scroggie said he had a “high degree of confidence” the company would continue supporting key neocloud customers, which make up part of Nextdc’s client base.

Nvidia, the world’s largest chipmaker, in September named Nextdc as one of eight infrastructure partners it was collaborating with to deliver up to a two-gigawatt AI factory buildout in Australia by 2027.

Earlier this month, Goodman Group and Digital Realty Trust Inc jointly bought a 9.9% stake in the company, opening the door to potential collaboration.

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 20): YTL Power International Bhd (KL:YTLPOWR) is planning further data centre investments after quarterly earnings from the segment surged nearly 133-fold year-on-year, while staying silent on the concerns raised amid the storm of controversy surrounding its global technology partner Nvidia Corp.

For the first quarter ended Sept 30, 2026 (1QFY2027), the data centre segment's profit before tax (PBT) jumped to RM139.54 million from RM1.05 million a year earlier, while revenue surged 491.35% to RM329.38 million from RM55.70 million, according to its latest results filing.

The data centre business has become the group's third-largest earnings contributor, behind power generation and water.

YTL Power, however, did not comment on the new restriction by the US on export of Nvidia chips to Malaysia.

YTL Power entered the data centre business in 2021 through the acquisition of a 50% stake in Dodid Pte Ltd, which owns a 12.5MW Tier-3 data centre in Singapore.

The group is a cloud and data centre partner of Nvidia, and operate data centres in Johor equipped with graphics processing units (GPUs) from the US chipmaker.

YTL Power has come under scrutiny after former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair. Media reports allege the woman Huang had an affair with was a spy who arranged for high-powered Nvidia chips to be diverted to China, in violation of US export curbs.

The woman is alleged to be a former executive of Singapore-based cloud firm Megaspeed International, which is reported to be a major customer of YTL Power.

However, it should be noted that there is no credible evidence implicating YTL Power in alleged chip diversion.

Queries to YTL Power on the matter from several media organisations, including *The Edge*, have gone unanswered.

And the silence continues in its latest quarterly earning report.

But the group is upbeat on its data centre prospects.

YTL Power said it has invested RM13.5 billion in the business and is looking to expand geographically beyond the Kulai Data Centre Park.

It plans to increase the capacity of its green data centre park to 1,200MW, of which 298MW has been contracted.

YTL Power is also developing a substantial portion of the Kulai Young Estate into a solar power facility with a generation capacity of up to 500MW to co-power the adjacent 600MW green data centre park. The first phase, involving a 215MWac solar power facility, has been implemented.

The surge in data centre earnings was insufficient to offset weaker earnings from its power generation and water businesses, with YTL Power's first-quarter net profit falling 7.98% year-on-year to RM460.62 million from RM500.57 million.

The decline was attributed to lower retail margins at its power generation business, while its water division was affected by higher maintenance costs and weaker earnings from the UK.

Quarterly revenue, however, rose 40.70% to RM7.54 billion from RM5.36 billion, mainly driven by higher electricity pool prices in its power generation business and the progressive completion and ramp-up in occupancy of additional data halls.

In the telecommunications sector, YTL Power said YTL Communications is looking to increase its subscriber base through affordable data plans, innovative 5G services, partnerships and collaborations. Its latest partnership with YTL AI Labs offers ILMUChat Pro plans free to YES subscribers.

YTL Power is also investing in Malaysia's AI ecosystem through its 70%-owned subsidiary YTL AI Labs, which owns and develops ILMU, a Malaysian large language model.

YTL Power's shares were unchanged at RM4 at Thursday's market close, giving the group a market capitalisation of approximately RM35 billion.

stories.title: Chip supply chain warns of broader disruption from new US export controls

stories.title: US chip curbs tilt Malaysia's data centres towards American giants as Nvidia scandal drags on

The controversy surrounding alleged diversion schemes has made Chinese-linked projects politically and commercially riskier, reshaping investment flows in one of Asia's fastest-growing markets.
stories.why_it_matters: Malaysia's data center boom faces a strategic inflection as Johor's proximity to Singapore becomes entangled with geopolitical compliance concerns, potentially bifurcating the market into US-aligned and China-adjacent ecosystems with divergent financing, tenant demand, and regulatory treatment.

stories.summary_zh: 美国持续限制Nvidia芯片对华出口，正推动马来西亚的数据中心发展转向美国hyperscale租户及其偏好的本地合作伙伴。围绕 alleged diversion schemes 的争议使与中国关联的项目在政治和商业上风险更高，重塑了这一亚洲增长最快市场之一的投资流向。

stories.content:
But the Asian country’s builders may be cushioned as other operators face supply and compliance risks

\[KUALA LUMPUR\] Malaysia’s data centre sector could shift further towards US tech giants as Washington’s tighter controls on advanced artificial intelligence chips and computing access put pressure on operators serving China-linked customers, analysts said.

Projects backed by US cloud giants are expected to cushion the impact of the tighter controls on Malaysian builders, while data centre operators serving China-linked customers face greater uncertainty over equipment supplies, compliance costs and expansion plans.

From Thursday (Nov 19), licences will be required to ship advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil to prevent smuggling, though qualifying US-headquartered firms are exempt.

The rule also restricts overseas data centres from supplying significant computing power to firms in Macau or arms-embargoed nations such as China, giving operators 90 days to secure licences.

The measures add pressure on Malaysia to safeguard its technology investment ambitions amid scrutiny of Singapore-based Megaspeed International and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix.

Economy Minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir said on Tuesday that recent controversies involving Nvidia do not alter Malaysia’s commitment to expanding its semiconductor and artificial intelligence sectors.

He emphasised that Malaysia’s broader manufacturing and chip export growth remains unaffected by the issue.

As at November, Malaysia has 55 operational data centres, out of 117 total approved projects tracked by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti).

Malaysia’s data centre boom has delivered a major boost to local construction firms and property developers partnering global tech giants. In 2026 alone, domestic data centre construction contract awards hit a record RM18.2 billion (US$4.4 billion), according to the Department of Statistics Malaysia.

Key beneficiaries include Sunway Construction Group, Gamuda, IJM Corp, Kerjaya Prospek, Sime Darby Property, YTL Corp and Eco World Development.

## Builders shielded by American clients

Kenanga Investment Bank’s head of research Peter Kong and analyst Lim Sin Kiat expect data centre demand to remain strong, but increasingly favour US-based customers and operators without China links.

They will be monitoring non-US operators’ expansion plans for a slowdown. At the same time, they noted Malaysia’s pipeline of 12.3 gigawatts for which electricity supply has been secured.

“We believe that hyperscalers facing roll-out restrictions in the US and planning to offshore could still see Malaysia benefit, cushioning the impact of this latest ruling,” they said.

Kenanga expects limited impact on builders under its coverage, as its clients predominantly comprise US hyperscalers, including Google, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft.

## Manageable near-term impact

RHB Investment Bank analyst Adam Bin Mohamed Rahim similarly anticipates a manageable impact on contractors in the near-to-medium term, citing their strong exposure to American technology groups.

He expects AI chip orders for data centres already under construction or nearing contract awards to remain largely intact over the next six to 12 months, supported by firm bookings from hyperscalers and co-location providers.

“The bigger concern is whether Nvidia can sustain the broader technological momentum of the AI industry under the new leadership,” he said.

He also noted that cloud providers may adopt multi-vendor strategies for future expansions, potentially accelerating graphics processing unit (GPU) supply diversification and reducing reliance on a single supplier.

## Impact on real estate sector

Meanwhile, the unfolding Megaspeed controversy carries direct implications for Malaysia’s industrial property and data centre real estate sectors, particularly in Johor, said Olive Tree Property Consultants founder and CEO Samuel Tan.

He noted that planned and under-construction facilities face potential delays if hardware shipment freezes disrupt project timelines.

“Financial institutions, turnkey contractors and tech partners may distance themselves from Megaspeed and MS Fusion to avoid secondary compliance penalties or reputational fallout,” he added.

He noted that securing the necessary long-term power allocations and planning approvals could become much more politically and bureaucratically sensitive.

While Johor has boomed into a premier South-east Asian data centre hub, high-profile scandals risk triggering tighter regional export licensing, he added.

Although a total AI chip ban remains unlikely, Tan warned that heightened audits, reporting duties and compliance overhead will significantly increase operating costs for data centre landlords and developers across the state.

## Putrajaya tightens data centre oversight

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Nov 13 there was no indication that chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed controversy had been exported from Malaysia.

On the same day, Miti separately clarified that it had never cleared Megaspeed or Speedmatrix. Routine verification visits did not constitute clearance, it said, describing Speedmatrix as a data centre tenant importing its own servers and AI chips.

Miti said it was working with the Customs Department to establish whether chips had been re-exported and whether any such shipments complied with Malaysian law.

Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Johari Abdul Ghani earlier said that Malaysia was drafting legislation requiring disclosure of data centre operators, facility locations, electricity consumption and imported GPU counts.

This would be separate from the planned Digital Infrastructure (Data Centre) Bill, which addresses broader sector governance.

Separately, Port Klang Free Zone chairman Lim Lip Eng said Speedmatrix’s proposed land lease would not proceed, after the company failed to sign the offer before it expired in early November. The proposed lease terms prohibited chip exports without prior approval from the authorities.

He said that Speedmatrix had applied to lease a parcel of land in the free zone in July, but did not execute the letter of offer within the stipulated period.

The offer contained strict terms and conditions, including “an express prohibition on the export of computer chips without prior approval from the relevant authorities”.

stories.title: Alibaba Cloud opens sixth data center in Malaysia

stories.content:
Alibaba Cloud, the cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) subsidiary of Alibaba Group, has added a third data center to its Johor public cloud region, growing the company’s data center footprint in Malaysia to six facilities.

The company announced the addition to the Johor region at its Qwen Conference Malaysia 2026. The third data center comes just six months after Alibaba Cloud launched its Johor region. The addition will grow the firm’s cloud infrastructure in Malaysia, complementing its three data centers in Kuala Lumpur, and provide additional capacity for organizations running cloud and AI workloads that need to be kept in the country.

Alibaba Cloud Intelligence General Manager of Malaysia, Choong Hon Keat, said that the firm sees its banking, telecommunications, digital payments, energy, and creative industry partners putting AI to work for their customers and teams.

“Our sixth data centre in Malaysia supports this work with more local cloud capacity and reflects our long-term commitment to helping Malaysian organisations of every size benefit from AI,” said Choong.

The opening of the sixth data center in Malaysia follows hot on the heels of w.media’s report that Alibaba Cloud launched in Amsterdam, Netherlands, at the end of October. Amsterdam became Alibaba Cloud’s fourth European region, joining Frankfurt in Germany, London in the UK, and Paris in France

The expansion forms part of the US$ 53 billion investment in AI and cloud infrastructure that Alibaba announced in 2025. To date, the company has launched 109 availability zones across 32 regions globally.

According to research from Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, the Asia-Pacific region has attracted some of the largest data center investments as governments race to accelerate digital infrastructure development and cloud providers expand regional capacity. However, as w.media reported this week, the US Department of Commerce has thrown a spanner in the works with the new interim final rule. The IFR outlines that exports of advanced US semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil will require a license and more robust oversight.

stories.content:
It is instructing that affected orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted

\[TAIPEI\] Taiwan’s TSMC is tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking technology, said two people familiar with the matter.

The move could close one of the last remaining routes for Chinese companies to produce powerful artificial intelligence processors, complicating Beijing’s efforts to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by TSMC.

The world’s largest contract chipmaker has instructed that affected orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted, unless customers obtain US export licences, the people said.

Chinese designers will generally be limited to older 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided their chips do not use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) or require advanced packaging, going by the TSMC guidance reviewed by the two people.

Most leading AI chips are produced using 7-nanometre processes or smaller, enabling faster and more energy-efficient performance.

HBM allows processors to handle the vast data volumes required by AI applications, while advanced packaging integrates chips and memory to boost computing power.

## US closes manufacturing route

The restrictions follow new US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday (Nov 19), removing a compliance route that had allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing services without individual export licences.

“TSMC is aware of and will comply with the new Bureau of Industry and Security regulations as applicable,” the company said in an e-mail to Reuters on Friday, adding it does not comment on market rumours.

Previously, it could check the computing power and other technical characteristics of certain Chinese chip designs to determine whether they fell outside US export controls.

Under the new rules, it can no longer use that verification process for affected Chinese customers. Their advanced chips are instead presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless an exception applies.

The *Financial Times* first reported on Thursday that TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following the new restrictions.

## China’s AI chip ambitions

The measures could particularly affect Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia’s processors, including independent chip designers and tech giants that have developed in-house chips.

A US government list of approved chip designers includes Nvidia, AMD, Apple and Taiwanese companies MediaTek and Realtek, but no mainland Chinese firms.

Some Chinese AI chip designers still had access to TSMC’s 7-nanometre manufacturing technology before Thursday, a separate source with direct knowledge of the matter said.

Reuters could not independently verify the arrangements under which those chips were manufactured.

TSMC’s guidance also requires closer scrutiny of customers’ operating locations, parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers and shipping routes, the two people familiar with the matter said.

The checks extend to orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or intermediaries, including entities in Taiwan, the US, Europe, Japan and South-east Asia. REUTERS

stories.title_zh: 总部位于新加坡的DayOne据称因data centre和市场担忧暂停US IPO计划
stories.content:
Investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for the AI boom’s digital infrastructure

\[HONG KONG\] DayOne Data Centres has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, people familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously.

But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.

Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.

The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.

Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the people said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment.

Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.

The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6 per cent in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.

Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17 per cent on its trading debut on Thursday, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.

Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever IPOs, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development, fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba.

The US this week put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators they will need a licence to purchase American tech hardware.

DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

stories.content:
Mistral, a provider of sovereign AI, has announced the opening of its Asia Pacific (APAC) headquarters in Singapore. The office will operate as an extended Science Hub for the company, focused on developing sovereign AI models for three areas: public sector, high-tech manufacturing, and robotics.

As per a press release, the new Science Hub in Singapore could help governments in APAC benefit from an open-weight approach to develop, customize and deploy AI within their own environments, aligned with local regulatory requirements and strategic priorities. This would include control across four dimensions: data sovereignty, ensuring sensitive information remains within designated boundaries; intelligence sovereignty, enabling customization and control; compute sovereignty, providing flexibility over infrastructure; and operational sovereignty, ensuring systems remain auditable and governable.

“The opening of Mistral’s Asia Pacific headquarters in Singapore as an extended Science Hub reflects our long-term commitment to building sovereign AI capabilities in the region, for the region,” said Arthur Mensch, Co-Founder and CEO, Mistral. “Our ambition is to establish Singapore as a strategic location for empowering governments and enterprises across Asia Pacific to retain ownership of their infrastructure and intelligence, and translate these into lasting economic value and industrial competitiveness.”

Mistral brings together frontier language models, physical AI, enterprise deployment and sovereign compute infrastructure in an integrated AI stack. This enables enterprises and public institutions to harness frontier AI while retaining control over their data, intellectual property and institutional knowledge. In high-tech manufacturing, Mistral aims to accelerate complex engineering simulations, optimize industrial processes and drive productivity and innovation. In robotics, Mistral is advancing intelligent models, including Robostral Navigate, an 8B model that enables robots to autonomously navigate complex environments using only a single RGB camera that is built entirely in-house, robot-agnostic and trained in simulation.

Singapore, in particular, has played a pivotal role in shaping Mistral’s global innovation strategy by pioneering AI development. Collaborations with DSO National Laboratories and HTX were among Mistral’s first model-customisation partnerships globally.

“Mistral’s Asia-Pacific headquarters and expansion of its research and development activities in Singapore reinforces our position as a hub for frontier AI innovation. This investment will accelerate AI development and innovation across key industries and create opportunities for Singaporeans to work on cutting-edge AI technologies. We look forward to growing Singapore’s AI ecosystem and capabilities together with Mistral,” said Pee Beng Kong, Executive Vice President, Singapore Economic Development Board.

“As HTX scales our impact on public safety, these kinds of partnerships will become even more crucial. With Mistral opening its new APAC HQ in Singapore, we look forward to even more seamless collaboration to help the Home Team keep Singapore safe and secure,” said Ang Chee Wee, Chief AI Officer and Assistant Chief Executive (Digital & Enterprise), HTX (Home Team Science and Technology Agency).

As part of its long-term commitment to APAC, Mistral also plans to more than double its workforce in Asia Pacific to 200 by 2027, building deep expertise across science, engineering, applied AI and robotics. This strategic investment in talent will support the Hub’s ambition to accelerate the development, training and real-world deployment of sovereign AI models.

stories.title: Nidec adapting cooling strategy for Vera Rubin era
stories.summary: Rising AI power density is pushing data centre operators towards higher-capacity liquid cooling, reshaping who suppliers like Nidec sell to.
stories.title_zh: Nidec为Vera Rubin时代调整冷却策略
stories.content:
Fri, 20th Nov 2026 (Today)
Nidec Corporation is adapting its data centre cooling strategy as Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin computing platform drives demand for higher-capacity liquid cooling systems and changes how equipment suppliers engage with infrastructure operators.

Nidec is seeing a shift towards in-row cooling distribution units (CDUs), which can deliver substantially greater cooling capacity than traditional in-rack systems, alongside demand for modular solutions that allow data centre operators to scale capacity according to their requirements.

Deputy Head of AI & IT Division SPMS at Nidec Corporation, Nobuyasu Nozawa, said the transition is reshaping the market for thermal management equipment and shifting relationships between suppliers, server manufacturers and data centre operators.

The Vera Rubin platform, which follows Nvidia's Blackwell architecture, is increasing the need for cooling infrastructure capable of supporting increasingly demanding AI workloads.

This is creating opportunities for manufacturers to supply larger cooling systems directly to data centre operators rather than relying exclusively on server manufacturers as customers.

"There is a significant shift happening from in-rack CDU into in-row CDU," Nozawa said.

Historically, in-rack CDUs have been a primary form factor for liquid cooling systems, with equipment installed within server racks and supplied through server manufacturers.

However, the move towards higher-capacity in-row systems is changing that model.

Unlike in-rack equipment, which is designed to fit within a server rack, in-row CDUs can occupy a footprint comparable to or larger than the server racks they support. Their size and capacity mean they are typically installed directly in the data hall rather than incorporated into server infrastructure.

As a result, cooling suppliers are increasingly engaging with data centre operators and infrastructure teams responsible for designing and managing facilities.

Nidec is now speaking more frequently with data centre customers, while continuing to work with server manufacturers.

The shift represents a change in the commercial structure of the market, as well as an evolution in cooling technology.

For suppliers, engaging directly with data centre operators can introduce different purchasing requirements and opportunities.

Instead of supplying equipment through a server manufacturer, vendors must increasingly account for the cooling requirements of entire facilities and the infrastructure supporting their AI deployments.

However, not every operator requires the full capacity offered by an in-row CDU.

Nidec is also developing modular cooling configurations for customers seeking capacity between that of conventional in-rack systems and larger in-row units.

Nozawa said some customers required more than the approximately 250 kilowatts available from an individual in-rack CDU but did not need a system capable of delivering two megawatts.

For these operators, Nidec offers a stackable CDU configuration that combines multiple smaller units to achieve a required cooling capacity.

Four 250kW CDUs can be combined to provide one megawatt of capacity, while five units can deliver 1.25MW.

The approach allows customers to select cooling capacity in increments rather than committing to a larger system that could exceed their immediate requirements.

Nidec is among a relatively small number of companies offering this type of stackable CDU solution alongside larger in-row systems.

The modular approach could provide an alternative for operators balancing the demands of AI infrastructure with the need to match cooling investment to deployment requirements.

As AI computing platforms increase in power density, data centre operators must consider not only the performance of their servers but also the infrastructure needed to remove heat reliably and efficiently.

Liquid cooling is becoming more important as conventional air-cooling approaches face limitations in handling the thermal output of high-performance computing systems.

For manufacturers such as Nidec, these developments are creating demand for a broader range of cooling equipment, from systems integrated into individual racks to larger installations serving multiple racks.

The transition towards higher-capacity systems also means thermal management suppliers must adapt their products and customer engagement strategies as data centre designs evolve.

Nidec's strategy combines larger in-row CDUs with modular stackable configurations, allowing it to address different cooling requirements as operators deploy increasingly powerful AI infrastructure.

Nozawa expects these changing requirements to influence how cooling equipment is specified, purchased and installed as the industry moves towards the next generation of AI computing platforms.

stories.title: Ransomware now a geopolitical disruption, says BlueVoyant VP
stories.summary: Ransomware attacks are evolving beyond traditional IT issues to become instruments of geopolitical disruption, according to Lorri Janssen-Anessi of BlueVoyant. Data centers must adopt business-wide resilience strategies to counter these advanced threats.
stories.title_zh: BlueVoyant副总裁：勒索软件已成为地缘政治 disruption 工具
stories.content:
Ransomware attacks are no longer merely isolated IT problems but have become instruments of geopolitical disruption, according to Lorri Janssen-Anessi, Vice President of Global Risk Operations at BlueVoyant.Data centers, increasingly critical to national infrastructure, face growing exposure to ransomware groups seeking operational disruption. A volatile geopolitical landscape further amplifies this threat, fuelling opportunistic cybercrime and targeting digital assets, networks, and facility systems.
### Evolving Threat Landscape

Traditional security models, focused on perimeter defence and isolated incident response, are proving inadequate against persistent, evolving ransomware activity. Modern attacks are increasing in frequency and sophistication, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), Janssen-Anessi noted.Nation-state actors are exploiting systemic weaknesses at scale, including unpatched vulnerabilities and weak identity controls. This challenges traditional siloed security models, especially as IT and operational technology (OT) systems converge in data centers, creating new attack paths.Ransomware attacks have also evolved beyond encryption. Threat actors now use “encryption-less extortion” tactics, focusing on data exfiltration and the threat of leaking sensitive information.AI accelerates these attacks by automating reconnaissance, credential theft, and large-scale extortion campaigns. These campaigns are increasingly deployed for political retaliation and reputational damage rather than purely financial gain.The distinction between criminal ransomware groups and state-sponsored actors has blurred due to overlapping tactics and infrastructure. This hybrid model obscures attribution, making responses more complex for data center operators caught in broader geopolitical tensions.
### Supply Chain and Resilience

The risks posed by nation-states are amplified in critical infrastructure environments. Ransomware-style attacks can impact building management systems, cooling infrastructure, and power management platforms, moving incidents beyond data loss to affecting service availability and safe facility operations.Attackers target third-party ecosystems rather than individual enterprises. Data center owners must secure privileged access to facility and OT systems, restrict third-party remote access, and maintain network segmentation.Decision-makers require increased visibility beyond direct suppliers, mapping data flows and dependencies across fourth- and fifth-party relationships. This includes understanding dependencies across hardware vendors, managed service providers, and connectivity partners.Addressing modern ransomware requires a shift from reactive defence to business-wide resilience. This means embedding cybersecurity into core business decision-making and involving cross-functional teams including legal, communications, HR, and facilities.Leadership accountability must increase, with boards and executives needing a clearer understanding of cyber risk. Janssen-Anessi stated that data center operators must assume disruption is a realistic scenario.Data center operators and digital infrastructure providers need to integrate cybersecurity, physical infrastructure security, supplier governance, and operational resilience into a unified risk management strategy.

Nvidia's commitments for neocloud agreements decreased to $32bn by the end of October 2026, from $36bn three months earlier.Interim Chief Executive Colette Kress stated that Nvidia will be "disciplined and selective" in supporting neoclouds. This change may affect how data centre operators' neocloud tenants secure financing, according to Capacity Media.The company reported record revenue of $115.8bn for the three months ending 25 October 2026, marking a 103 per cent year-on-year increase. Data centre revenue rose 110 per cent to $107.6bn, with Nvidia guiding to $130bn, plus or minus 3 per cent, for the current quarter.Under former CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia used its balance sheet to support customers through equity stakes in AI labs and neoclouds, promises to buy back unsold cloud capacity, and guarantees on data centre leases. Nvidia’s guarantees allowed lenders to price debt partly against Nvidia’s credit, which was crucial for young, heavily indebted neoclouds lacking investment-grade ratings.A reduction in Nvidia's support could lead to higher borrowing costs, longer discounted contracts, or slower expansion for neoclouds. Nvidia’s guarantees are conditional, taking effect only once a neocloud has secured financing, deployed capacity, made it operational, and had it accepted by Nvidia. None of the remaining $32bn in commitments falls due before fiscal 2028.Analysis from Ornn suggests Nvidia will continue supporting strategically important customers, but on tighter terms. Credit risk for neoclouds is shifting from the chipmaker to private credit, insurers, and infrastructure funds, which impacts operator leases. stories.title: Data centre emissions to rise 70 per cent by 2030, IEA warns
stories.summary: The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects a 70 per cent increase in data centre emissions by 2030. This rise is attributed to the growing reliance on fossil fuels to power data centres amid the AI boom.
stories.title_zh: IEA警告：数据中心排放量到2030年将上升70%
stories.content:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warns that data centre emissions could rise by 70 per cent by 2030, according to its latest World Energy Outlook.This increase is driven by the continued growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) sector. The IEA forecasts global data centre electricity consumption will double to approximately 1,000TWh by the end of the decade.A significant concern is the power sources for this growth. The IEA estimates that coal and natural gas will remain major electricity sources for data centres for years. These two sources currently account for around 60 per cent of the electricity physically supplying data centres worldwide.Many data centres consider gas-fired generators as an alternative when grid capacity is insufficient. These generators are relatively cheap and provide a reliable electricity stream.Renewable generation is expected to expand substantially. The tech industry is already the largest corporate purchaser of renewable electricity. Nearly half of global commercial data centre electricity demand is now covered by renewable power purchase agreements (PPAs).However, PPAs do not guarantee renewable electricity availability when a data centre needs it. Operators can buy enough renewable electricity to match annual consumption while grids still rely on fossil fuels.The IEA expects natural gas and renewables to account for approximately 80 per cent of the additional electricity generation required by data centres between 2025 and 2030. The generation mix varies significantly by region.In the United States, natural gas is projected to supply around 60 per cent of data centre electricity by 2030. China is expected to remain heavily dependent on coal, which could provide more than half.The European Union presents a different scenario, with renewables projected to supply around two-thirds of data centre electricity by 2030. The UK government aims for clean sources to account for at least 95 per cent of Great Britain’s electricity generation by 2030.Securing sufficient grid capacity remains a challenge in the UK. Some developers are considering alternative power sources to bring projects online sooner. A proposed 72MW data centre near Reading plans to initially use natural gas fuel cells due to unavailable grid capacity.The developer's modelling suggests that long-term gas use would result in substantially higher emissions than switching to grid electricity. MPs have launched an inquiry into the environmental impact of UK data centres, examining electricity and water requirements.

stories.summary_zh: 行业分析师警告称，美国扩大半导体出口限制可能减缓东南亚的数据中心建设，马来西亚和泰国被认定为风险敞口特别大的市场。虽然colocation和云服务的终端用户需求保持强劲，但设备供应商因芯片供应中断面临最严峻的收入风险。

stories.content:
While demand for operators remains strong, they warn that chip suppliers are at the biggest risk

\[SINGAPORE\] Washington’s new curbs on advanced artificial intelligence chips could slow down the next phase of growth for South-east Asia’s data centre build-out, analysts said.

Malaysia and Thailand face greater risks from the restrictions due to their exposure to non-US data centre customers, while Singapore could see delays to its next wave of data centre development, they added.

The rule, issued by the US Department of Commerce on Monday (Nov 16), requires licences for advanced AI chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, with exemptions for US-headquartered companies.

The five countries account for about 7 to 9 per cent of the world’s operational data centre capacity at about 5.5 gigawatt (GW) of IT load, noted a DBS Group Research note released on Tuesday.

CGS International (CGSI) expects the ruling to benefit US hyperscalers, while DBS also noted that the rule could shift AI infrastructure investment “towards jurisdictions and operators facing fewer regulatory hurdles”.

“China-facing AI projects and independent graphics processing unit (GPU)-cloud operators face higher execution risks,” it noted in a report.

## Malaysia and Thailand face greater exposure risk

Over in Malaysia, of the 8.4 GW of data centre power supply agreements signed with the government as at June, about 30 per cent is linked to US-headquartered companies.

The remaining users are “less clear”, noted the research house.

Meanwhile, colocation demand in Thailand data centres is also expected to slow down as the data centre operators that serve Chinese tech companies have to obtain US export licences when importing advanced AI chips from the US.

In Singapore, CGSI analysts said it believes the build-out for the second Data Centre Call for Application (DC-CFA2) and the upcoming data-centre park in Jurong Island “could be deferred”.

The research house cited “the potential souring of sentiments and demand”, following the new US rule as the primary reason for the slowdown.

In Singapore, four data centre operators – Digital Realty, Equinix, STT GDC and Keppel – were each provisionally allocated 50 megawatts (MW) under the DC-CFA2 tender in August.

Cristina Brayton-Lewis, partner at law firm White & Case, expects some “chilling effect” on data centre operators in Asean.

As a result of the new rule, some projects “may not be able to obtain necessary licences”, she said. “Other projects may be able to secure licences, but may face delays in licensing or potentially burdensome licensing conditions.”

Foo Zhiwei, analyst at Macquarie Capital, expects a “slowdown, not a halt”, as operators deal with the extra licensing requirements and additional know-your-customer checks.

DBS Group Research noted that the licensing requirements could delay GPU shipments and AI deployments.

The effects will be felt most among non-US cloud operators, noted DBS.

## Operators still report strong demand

Serene Nah, managing director and head of Asia-Pacific at Digital Realty, said that the operator is still choosing tenants for its upcoming SIN13 data centre facility.

“We’re approached by so many people because we have the 50 MW, so we have to pick,” she said.

She added that the SIN13 data centre will host mostly AI inference and high-performance computing. Therefore, the company may lean towards companies that can more easily import GPUs under the new rules.

That said, she noted that the new rules means that the operator will “need to be more selective” of the customers it selects for the data centre.

Keppel, another of the four awarded capacity through the DC-CFA2, said it does not expect the measures to have a significant impact on its data centre business in Singapore.

“Most of our Singapore data centres, including the floating data centre under construction, are predominantly committed to US-based hyperscalers,” said a Keppel spokesperson.

Despite the restrictions, CGSI expects an upside for Singapore operators.

“(Singapore) could benefit over time if it establishes itself as a trusted computing hub for compliant workloads and hyperscalers,” the research house noted.

## Chip suppliers at risk

While demand for operators remains strong, analysts warned that chip suppliers are at the biggest risk.

AEM is directly exposed through its AI and high-performance computing customers, while UMS, Frencken and Venture could be impacted indirectly, noted CGSI.

“We think the key risk to earnings is a slower and more measured demand pace from customers, which could potentially affect earnings growth pace over FY2027 and (potentially) FY2028,” noted the research house.

However, DBS said that the impact on equipment makers is limited.

“The measures primarily target advanced computing chips rather than equipment,” said DBS, noting that UMS and Frencken are less affected.

“While slower AI capacity expansion could eventually weigh on wafer fab equipment spending, UMS and Frencken are less affected in the near term.”

However, DBS noted that Venture might be affected, given its exposure to AI infrastructure hardware, networking and test equipments

Overall, CGSI expects investments to slow down mainly “as investors await licensing clarity”.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Tuesday said Singapore can facilitate US checks on companies and how advanced chips brought into the country are deployed, if Washington has concerns.

He noted that a large portion of chips recorded, as sales to Singapore never enter the country.

“Only a small volume of those chips’ directly comes into Singapore,” said PM Wong.

stories.content:
The Commerce Department approved applications to sell more than 3.4 million chips to the firms, lawmakers say

#### Sudeshna Dhar

\[WASHINGTON\] Lawmakers released confidential information on Thursday (Nov 19) showing that the Commerce Department had approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies for the year, as of May 11, including several firms on a list of Chinese military companies maintained by the Pentagon.

The department had received applications to sell more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese companies as at that date, lawmakers said. It approved 75,000 AI chips for Alibaba, a Chinese AI giant that *The New York Times* reported this week has ties with a military-linked laboratory.

The release also showed that Nvidia had submitted an application in April to sell more than 40,000 of its advanced H200 chips to a company tied to Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the executive who US intelligence has concluded was a Chinese asset who had an affair with the former Nvidia CEO.

The company – New Century Lettall Data Service – is part of a network of Chinese companies with ties to Megaspeed and Huang. Its historical ownership traces back in part to an investment firm controlled by Huang’s sister, where Kang Wei, whom Huang often introduced as her husband, was also executive director.

The Commerce Department also approved 150,000 chips for Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent and its subsidiaries; 43,000 for Baidu, another Chinese AI firm; and 4,000 for BYD, a carmaker, the lawmakers said.

They were Nvidia’s H200 chips and the equivalent from the chipmaker AMD, the MI325X.

The lawmakers from the House Foreign Affairs Committee took special note of the Commerce Department’s approval of sales to the companies Maginfra, Beijing New Matrix Information Technologies and Aivres Systems.

The committee cited reporting by *The New York Times* that had raised questions about those firms because of their ties to sanctioned entities and noted that many of the licence requests from Nvidia had listed the companies as entities that might install the systems in data centres.

Two reports from *The New York Times* first raised concerns about the firms in September and October, saying that Aivres was the subsidiary of a sanctioned Chinese firm that had exported billions of dollars of advanced Nvidia chips to Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal.

*The New York Times* reporters also visited the China offices of Maginfra and New Matrix and found them to be empty. No one present had heard of the firms, and scant information existed about them online, raising questions about whether they really existed.

The revelations that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with Alice Huang, along with a second woman at Nvidia, forced him to step down last week. The Justice and Commerce Departments said this week that Megaspeed was under criminal investigation for potentially smuggling chips into China.

The incident has sparked criticism from lawmakers that the Trump administration, and the Commerce Department in particular, did too little to police the flow of sensitive technology to China.

Officials both in the administration and on Capitol Hill have criticised the department for maintaining close ties to Nvidia, which it is charged with regulating.

The Commerce Department has defended its processes, saying that it closely follows national security regulations. Every Nvidia and AMD application also stated that the proposed transfer posed a low risk of diversion, the committee’s release said.

John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, said that all the company’s shipments were legal and authorised by the government, and that, despite receiving some licences, Nvidia had already stopped shipping H200s to China.

Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company, he said.

A spokesperson for AMD said the company complied with applicable U.S. laws and regulations and had a rigorous process to ensure compliance.

A spokesperson for the Commerce Department said the disclosure was evidence of the department’s transparency with Congress about licensing activity. Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. government agencies, he said.

President Donald Trump approved the sale of the H200 to China in December under unusual conditions. He required the chips, which are assembled in Taiwan, to be routed through the United States on their way to China, so that the government could collect a 25 per cent tariff on their value and perform a security check.

Wary of the arrangement and eager to promote its own technology, the Chinese government ended up approving few purchases from its firms.

Nvidia said in its earnings this week that it would halt sales of its H200 chips to China, though it did not give a reason for the move.

In its statement, the House Foreign Affairs Committee said that withholding the information was “contrary to the national interest”.

The committee plans to hold hearings next month with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeff Kessler, who has had a special role in approving license applications.

Rep Brian Mast who chairs the committee, called Maginfra and New Matrix “fake companies”, and said that if the Commerce Department granted approvals to the firms, “obviously that is of tremendous concern to us”, he said.

Rep Gregory W Meeks said that the public deserved to know how decisions to sell technology to China were made, and that Congress needed to “conduct rigorous oversight”.

“Over the past month, the administration’s handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk,” he said. NYTIMES
